title: Booking Recovery Loop
user: Solo tutors, coaches, and consultants who sell paid sessions and need every abandoned or at-risk booking to become a completed, paid appointment. Paying customer: a one-to-five-person practice; wedge: conversion and delivery certainty after the booking link, at $29/month.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A tutoring side-hustle operator says scheduling tools feel bloated, clients get confused and text anyway; a legal consultant wants a booking experience that converts and includes Stripe.
A self-hosted Cal.com user reports that 24-hour and one-hour appointment reminder workflows were created but never executed.

recurrence: Independent solo-service complaints cover booking-page friction, payments, and reminder delivery; a missed paid session is immediately lost revenue.
current_workaround: Use Calendly/Cal.com plus Stripe plus manual texts, then check email logs when a reminder or booking goes missing.
incumbents_and_gap: Calendly, Cal.com, SavvyCal, and Stripe solve calendar slots or payment individually. They do not make the conversion-to-attendance chain, including fallback recovery, the accountable product for tiny practices.
smallest_useful_product: Branded paid-session page, Stripe deposit, reminder delivery receipt, and an automatic SMS/email fallback when a booking is abandoned or a reminder bounces. Non-goals: calendar replacement, CRM, or marketplace discovery.
success_measure: In 60 days, pilot practices recover at least 10% of abandoned booking attempts or reduce paid-session no-shows by 20% versus their prior 60 days.
monetization: subscription — $29/month per practice is justified by recovering a single session and covers messaging delivery.
constraints: Obtain consent for SMS/email, use Stripe-hosted payment collection, encrypt client contact data, and support deletion/export.
why_distinct: The product owns measurable booking recovery and reminder proof, not just a public availability page.

title: Class Capacity Truth
user: Small language schools and tutoring centres running paid group assessments or classes who need the capacity shown to families to match real seats. Paying customer: school operations lead; wedge: trustworthy seat inventory and waitlist conversion at $99/month.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The scheduling discussion identifies group bookings and reminders as paid add-ons and says generic scheduling products are rigid, impersonal, and overkill for small businesses.
An English language school reports Cal.com showing only one or two places available while all places remained available, explicitly tying the defect to booking more level checks.

recurrence: The same class-booking problem appears as both a small-business product complaint and a school operator's revenue-impacting seat-count defect.
current_workaround: Keep a spreadsheet alongside a booking tool, manually confirm every group booking, and call waitlisted families one at a time.
incumbents_and_gap: Calendly and Cal.com offer group events; full school-information systems are broad and costly. Neither is a lightweight capacity truth layer that reconciles seats, blocks oversell, and converts a waitlist for small schools.
smallest_useful_product: Connect one calendar, define class capacity and cutoff rules, expose a parent booking page, reconcile bookings every few minutes, and send one-click released-seat offers. Non-goals: student records, grading, or a full SIS.
success_measure: A pilot has zero incorrect seat displays for 90 days and fills at least 25% of released places from its waitlist within 24 hours.
monetization: subscription — $99/month per school is small relative to one filled assessment group and supports monitoring and notifications.
constraints: Protect child and parent data, minimize data retention, provide role-based access, and support regional privacy requirements.
why_distinct: It is a narrow capacity-reconciliation and waitlist revenue product, not another school management suite.

title: Clinic Slot Safety
user: Independent outpatient and therapy clinics that schedule by hand and need staff to move an appointment without breaking provider, room, duration, or eligibility rules. Paying customer: clinic manager; wedge: explainable safe rescheduling at $249/month.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The therapy discussion describes access barriers and patient-therapist fit as major friction; a commenter cites $150–250 sessions and long treatment timelines, making lost slots consequential.
Medplum specifies drag-and-drop appointment editing with on-drop validation because direct scheduler placement must be validated against booking rules.

recurrence: Appointment access and high-value therapy sessions create a recurring operational cost; healthcare platform work explicitly prioritizes validated rescheduling.
current_workaround: Reception staff inspect calendars, phone providers, then move appointments manually or leave open slots unused to avoid conflict.
incumbents_and_gap: Jane, SimplePractice, and enterprise EHR schedulers bundle many clinical workflows. Small clinics still lack a standalone, explainable pre-flight check that can sit alongside their existing calendar.
smallest_useful_product: Calendar connector, rule builder for provider/room/service constraints, drag-to-propose move, human-readable conflict explanation, and patient confirmation link. Non-goals: EHR, diagnosis, claims, or clinical decision support.
success_measure: Pilot clinics complete 90% of reschedules without a back-and-forth call and record zero rule-violating moves for 90 days.
monetization: subscription — $249/month per location is defensible against a handful of avoided empty clinician hours.
constraints: Health data requires jurisdiction-specific compliance, BAAs where applicable, least-privilege calendar scopes, audit logs, and no clinical recommendations.
why_distinct: It is a safety layer for rescheduling, deliberately not a new practice-management or therapy product.

title: MTD Evidence Rail
user: UK sole traders, tutors, and micro-club operators facing Making Tax Digital quarterly updates who need every expense and invoice traceable to a reviewable digital record. Paying customer: non-accountant sole trader; wedge: quarterly evidence readiness at £15/month.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The Ask HN author notes April 2026/2027 MTD thresholds and says freelancers and tutors still use spreadsheets or notes because Xero feels heavy; commenters say mainstream tools are hard to set up.
A user requests URL-backed receipt links because uploading documents into the invoicing product is not a workable way to connect receipts to expenses.

recurrence: A regulatory deadline turns scattered records into a recurring quarterly deadline, while invoice users still need document linkage outside accounting suites.
current_workaround: Keep paper or photo receipts, enter totals into spreadsheets, and assemble accountant evidence shortly before each quarterly update.
incumbents_and_gap: Xero, QuickBooks, FreeAgent, and HMRC-compatible filing tools are comprehensive. The gap is a calm, evidence-first rail for people who do not need a general ledger all day.
smallest_useful_product: Receipt capture, invoice/expense timeline, bank-CSV matching suggestions, missing-evidence queue, and accountant export mapped to quarterly periods. Non-goals: filing on behalf of users, tax advice, payroll, or full double-entry accounting.
success_measure: At least 80% of pilot users finish their quarterly evidence pack before the final week of the period, with fewer than three unlinked transactions per quarter.
monetization: subscription — £15/month aligns with a regulated recurring job and remains far below full-suite pricing.
constraints: Do not give tax advice or claim HMRC filing certification until accredited; protect financial documents and retain audit history with user-controlled export/deletion.
why_distinct: The v1 sells evidence completeness before filing, rather than trying to clone an accounting package.

title: AP-Ready Invoice
user: Freelancers and small studios paid by corporate finance departments who need invoices accepted on the first attempt and need to see who has the next action. Paying customer: independent professional; wedge: accounts-payable readiness and follow-through at $19/month.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A freelancer says FreshBooks is overkill and clients rarely use its payment links; they export PDFs and send them to AP/finance email addresses anyway.
Invoice Ninja users request a company/group/client selector in the client portal, showing that a simple invoice-to-one-client model breaks down for real billing relationships.

recurrence: Freelancers repeatedly confront finance-team workflows after creating an invoice, while invoice systems continue to receive requests for more complex payer relationships.
current_workaround: Export a PDF, email AP manually, keep PO/tax/bank details in notes, and chase status through email threads.
incumbents_and_gap: FreshBooks, QuickBooks, Invoice Ninja, and payment links generate invoices. Their primary workflow is issuing or collecting, not a preflight checklist and receipt trail tailored to corporate AP handoff.
smallest_useful_product: Reusable client AP profiles, invoice preflight for required fields/PO/tax/bank details, branded PDF/email package, secure status link, and escalation timeline. Non-goals: merchant processing, bookkeeping, or a general CRM.
success_measure: In pilots, 85% of invoices pass the recipient's first AP review and median time-to-first-status drops by 30%.
monetization: subscription — $19/month is tied to predictable cash collection and avoids a percentage of freelance income.
constraints: Secure bank and tax identifiers, never impersonate an AP system, and make delivery/audit logs exportable.
why_distinct: It specializes in the handoff after invoice creation, rather than becoming another invoicing ledger.

title: Subcontractor Margin Chain
user: Boutique agencies that deliver through freelancers and subcontractors but need to see end-client commitments, subcontractor cost, approval, and invoice status in one job chain. Paying customer: agency owner; wedge: job-level margin protection at $79/month.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The author reports interviews with 60+ freelancers, creators, and small agencies who lose 20–30% of time and revenue to work split across Gmail/WhatsApp, Notion, payment links, and spreadsheets.
A feature request asks for end-client/sub-client relationships across clients, projects, tasks, and invoices for subcontracted work.

recurrence: Both qualitative agency interviews and an invoicing feature request point to the same missing link between the buyer, delivery partner, work, and cash.
current_workaround: Create separate client/project records, keep subcontractor rates in spreadsheets, and reconcile profitability only after invoices are paid.
incumbents_and_gap: Harvest, Bonsai, HoneyBook, and Invoice Ninja cover pieces of time, invoices, or portals. They do not make a nested end-client-to-subcontractor margin chain the core operational record.
smallest_useful_product: A job chain with end client, agency client, subcontractors, approved scope, committed cost, invoice milestones, and margin-at-risk alerts. Non-goals: payroll, marketplace hiring, general project management, or accounting.
success_measure: Pilot agencies record 95% of subcontracted jobs before work starts and catch at least one margin-at-risk job per quarter before invoicing.
monetization: subscription — $79/month per agency is justified by protecting one project's margin and scales by active job chains, not seats.
constraints: Protect contractor rates and client identities with role-based access; do not calculate payroll tax or make employment classifications.
why_distinct: The central object is a commercial delivery chain, not a generic task board or freelancer marketplace.

title: Client Intake Proof
user: Small professional-service firms that must collect documents, decisions, and scope before beginning client work. Paying customer: agency or accounting-firm operations lead; wedge: provable intake completeness at $49/month.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A solo engineering lab built a self-hosted client portal after finding HoneyBook expensive and fragmented; its essentials are file sharing, project tracking, and invoicing under the firm's brand.
Plane's intake open count fails to update after accept, decline, or duplicate, demonstrating how an intake queue can misstate the work still awaiting action.

recurrence: Client-portal fragmentation and unreliable intake status both create a costly ambiguity: whether work is truly ready to start.
current_workaround: Send a branded portal or email checklist, chase attachments in email, then manually tell the delivery team that the project is ready.
incumbents_and_gap: HoneyBook, Dubsado, Plane, and generic portals offer broad workflows. The missing focused artifact is a client-visible, immutable proof that every prerequisite was supplied, waived, or explicitly accepted.
smallest_useful_product: Template-driven intake checklist, magic-link document requests, required-field validation, client acknowledgements, internal exception approval, and a signed readiness packet. Non-goals: project board, e-signature platform, or file-drive replacement.
success_measure: At least 90% of pilot engagements start with a complete readiness packet, and operations reports 30% fewer pre-start clarification messages.
monetization: subscription — $49/month per firm is tied to every new engagement and avoids per-client portal pricing.
constraints: Encrypt uploads, support retention policies and export, use legal e-signature providers if required, and prohibit sensitive identity collection by default.
why_distinct: It sells a readiness proof packet and exception trail, not a broad white-label client portal.

title: Cross-Client Demand Desk
user: Small agencies with several client projects who need to decide which incoming request deserves scarce team capacity today. Paying customer: agency owner or delivery lead; wedge: cross-client prioritization with commercial context at $79/month.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A solo technical founder describes repeatedly shipping without traction and asks how to make marketing decisions without an unaffordable hire or risky co-founder commitment.
Plane users explicitly say teams working in multiple projects cannot prioritize intake across them because there is no unified cross-project view.

recurrence: The need to allocate limited effort is direct in multi-project intake, while small operators need every commercial action to count.
current_workaround: Review separate project boards, Slack/email requests, and revenue notes in a weekly meeting; urgent clients win by interruption.
incumbents_and_gap: Asana, Linear, Plane, ClickUp, and Monday aggregate tasks but are not designed to rank agency demand by client value, renewal risk, committed scope, and delivery capacity.
smallest_useful_product: One inbound queue across client workspaces, request type/value/risk fields, capacity-aware ranking, and a weekly decision log explaining what was deferred. Non-goals: task execution, time tracking, CRM, or automated client promises.
success_measure: In a 90-day pilot, 80% of accepted requests have a recorded commercial reason and unplanned client interrupts fall by 25%.
monetization: subscription — $79/month per agency replaces a recurring management meeting and protects retention-critical work.
constraints: Treat commercial scoring as editable advice, protect client data with workspace isolation, and provide a transparent export of rank inputs.
why_distinct: It is a commercial demand-control desk, not another cross-project task list.

title: Multicurrency VAT Close
user: Small B2C SaaS operators already on Stripe who sell internationally and need a month-end VAT/sales-tax evidence pack that reconciles currency and remittance status. Paying customer: founder-led finance team; wedge: close readiness at $79/month.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A B2C SaaS founder says moving existing Stripe subscribers to a merchant-of-record is non-trivial and distinguishes tax data collection from registration, filing, and remittance.
Invoice Ninja users request date-aware historical exchange rates because a single current rate is inadequate for invoices and expenses.

recurrence: International subscription operators face a monthly close and periodic filing cycle, while historical-currency treatment remains a concrete accounting-system gap.
current_workaround: Export Stripe CSVs, use a tax calculation service, copy exchange rates into spreadsheets, and hire accountants to reconcile exceptions.
incumbents_and_gap: Stripe Tax, Avalara, Quaderno, Paddle, and accountants each handle pieces. The unresolved wedge is a read-only close packet for an existing Stripe stack that surfaces filing/remittance and FX evidence gaps without forcing migration.
smallest_useful_product: Stripe read-only import, jurisdiction/currency reconciliation, dated-rate evidence, registration/remittance checklist, exception queue, and accountant-ready monthly export. Non-goals: calculating legal tax liability, filing returns, merchant-of-record service, or payment processing.
success_measure: Pilots produce a reconciled close pack in under two hours and reduce accountant follow-up exceptions by 40% after three closes.
monetization: subscription — $79/month fits a recurring close and is cheaper than manual reconciliation time; higher tiers can price by monthly transaction volume.
constraints: Read-only financial integrations, no tax advice or filing representation, jurisdictional disclaimers, encrypted records, and immutable exported evidence.
why_distinct: It complements an existing payment stack with evidence and exception control rather than competing as tax engine or merchant of record.

title: Field Job Proof Pack
user: Solo carpenters and small trades businesses that need a customer-approved scope, visit record, completion evidence, and payment request without buying a full field-service suite. Paying customer: owner-operator; wedge: dispute-resistant job closeout at $49/month.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A solo carpenter says Jobber cost $150+/month and was too bloated; they wanted only invoicing, scheduling, and client management at a flat $5/month.
A Cal.com user reports that a configured appointment type was absent from the booking calendar, a direct example of a scheduled customer visit becoming unreliable.

recurrence: Tradespeople face a clear price/bloat complaint, and even booking infrastructure can fail at the point a customer expects a visit.
current_workaround: Use a calendar, text messages, phone photos, notes, and a separate invoice; reconstruct proof only when a customer disputes scope or completion.
incumbents_and_gap: Jobber, Housecall Pro, Tradify, and ServiceTitan are broad operations suites. The gap is a low-admin closeout packet that turns each paid job into reusable scope-and-completion proof.
smallest_useful_product: Mobile job card, customer-approved scope/change request, timestamped before/after photos, visit check-in, completion acknowledgement, and invoice handoff. Non-goals: route optimization, payroll, dispatch center, or marketplace leads.
success_measure: Pilot owners create proof packs for 75% of completed jobs and cut payment disputes or clarification visits by 25% over a quarter.
monetization: subscription — $49/month per business is below current field-suite entry points and defensible through fewer disputed jobs.
constraints: Photo metadata and customer addresses need consent, encrypted storage, retention controls, and offline-tolerant mobile capture.
why_distinct: The core artifact is a customer-shareable proof pack, not an attempt to clone dispatch-heavy field service software.

title: Service Reminder Receipts
user: Trades and recurring-service businesses that book follow-up visits and need to prove a reminder was delivered before a costly no-show. Paying customer: owner-manager with recurring appointments; wedge: durable reminder delivery receipts at $69/month.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A new free field-service product for tradespeople appeared on HN, confirming active demand for a focused alternative to expensive operational software.
A self-hosted Cal.com license holder reports workflow emails not being sent despite SMTP configuration, exposing a gap between scheduling and dependable customer notification.

recurrence: Focused field-service alternatives continue to appear, while reminder delivery itself can silently fail and turn into avoidable empty visits.
current_workaround: Trust calendar emails, manually text customers, or discover a missed reminder only after a no-show and a support complaint.
incumbents_and_gap: Jobber, Housecall Pro, Calendly, and Cal.com offer reminders as a feature. They rarely provide a channel-independent receipt, fallback policy, and no-show evidence workflow for a small service business.
smallest_useful_product: Import upcoming visits, send consented SMS/email reminders, verify delivery/open/reply where supported, trigger configured fallbacks, and produce a visit-level receipt. Non-goals: scheduling UI, dispatch, payments, or marketing campaigns.
success_measure: Pilot businesses obtain a delivery receipt for 95% of reminders and reduce unconfirmed no-shows by 20% in 90 days.
monetization: subscription — $69/month plus pass-through message use is justified by avoiding even a few wasted callouts.
constraints: SMS consent and opt-out are mandatory; respect regional messaging laws, retain only necessary delivery metadata, and never infer fault from an unopened message.
why_distinct: It is a notification accountability layer, not another booking or field-service system.

title: Decision Receipt Inbox
user: Small product and service teams collecting customer feedback who need every request to end in an explicit decision, owner, response, and audit trail. Paying customer: product or client-success lead; wedge: feedback-to-decision accountability at $49/month.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A customer-feedback product launched with flat pricing and no per-user billing, signalling dissatisfaction with feedback-tool pricing models for small teams.
An n8n user reports that human approval buttons were not rendered in built-in editor chat, showing that a workflow with an intended decision point can fail to collect the decision at all.

recurrence: Small teams seek predictable feedback-tool pricing, and human-in-the-loop approval remains operationally brittle even in workflow systems.
current_workaround: Collect feedback in forms, Intercom, email, or spreadsheets; discuss it in meetings; then answer customers manually with no durable link to the decision.
incumbents_and_gap: Canny, Productboard, Fider, Intercom, and n8n collect, prioritize, or automate pieces. The gap is a compact decision receipt that proves an owner made a response-worthy choice and closes the customer loop.
smallest_useful_product: Shared feedback inbox, duplicate clustering, decision buttons with required rationale/owner/due date, customer update templates, and immutable decision receipts. Non-goals: roadmapping, AI-generated feature decisions, help desk, or generic automation builder.
success_measure: Within 60 days, pilots attach an explicit decision to 80% of feedback items and send a customer-facing outcome for 60% of high-value requests.
monetization: subscription — $49/month flat for a small team answers per-seat pricing frustration and maps to an ongoing customer-retention workflow.
constraints: Do not expose customer identities across workspaces; allow redaction and export; clearly label automated clustering as assistance, never as a decision.
why_distinct: It focuses on the accountable outcome and customer reply, not on collecting votes or producing an AI roadmap.
